summary:
Sky Time Machine is an interactive web application inspired by NASA’s SPHEREx mission which provides an accessible way to compare astronomical images. The web application was created using Python, Streamlit and Astropy. Users can view changing infrared images using a Dual Observation Viewer containing Blink Mode, Swipe Comparison and Difference Image. There is also a Spectral Explorer which mimics the 102 near-infrared bands of SPHEREx.

Identification of moving/variable objects across epochs is a challenge in astronomy. Due to background constant stars it becomes difficult to see small changes between images and can require complex processing pipelines. Sky Time Machine uses both a user-friendly visual method and Candidate Detection System which uses coordinate alignment, image subtraction, median absolute deviation noise calculation and positive/negative peak matching to create potential candidate objects within the simulated data sets.

This application brings the complex image processing techniques used in astronomy to life for everyone! Giving users a fun way to see real concepts within space missions. Students, Citizen Scientists and anyone with a curious mind can explore a changing universe.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

Sky Time Machine is an interactive web application that allows users to explore and compare astronomical observations in a more accessible way. Inspired by NASA's SPHEREx mission, the application helps users understand changes in the infrared sky through an interactive browser-based platform. Users can enter celestial coordinates, such as Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec), or choose specific astronomical targets like Barnard's Star and WISE 0855. The application processes infrared data across 102 spectral bands and displays visualizations of different wavelengths, including spectral energy distributions (SEDs). It also provides an Image Subtraction feature that compares two observation frames to help identify possible moving objects, such as asteroids and brown dwarfs.

2. What benefits does it have?

The main benefit of Sky Time Machine is that it makes astronomical data easier to access and understand without requiring users to install complicated astronomy software. Everything can be explored directly through a web browser, making it more convenient for students, researchers, and astronomy enthusiasts. The application also provides interactive controls that allow users to switch between different infrared bands and observe how astronomical objects appear across different wavelengths. In addition, its URL-sharing feature allows users to share specific sky coordinates with others, making it easier to discuss observations, learn together, and collaborate.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The main goal of Sky Time Machine is to make space data more accessible to everyone, especially students, citizen scientists, and people who are interested in astronomy but may not have a technical background. Through this project, users can explore astronomical observations and learn more about infrared astronomy without needing advanced programming skills. It also aims to support early astronomical research by providing tools to compare observations and identify potential moving objects, such as asteroids and brown dwarfs. Besides that, Sky Time Machine can be used as an educational tool to help students understand the electromagnetic spectrum, infrared wavelengths, and how scientists observe the universe.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

I developed Sky Time Machine using Python as the main programming language and Streamlit to build the interactive web application. For data processing and visualization, I used NumPy, Pandas, and Matplotlib to handle astronomical information and present it through graphs and visual displays. I also used Git and GitHub to manage the project files and organize the development process. For deployment, I used Streamlit Cloud so that the application can be accessed publicly through a website without requiring users to run the code on their own computers.

5. How is your project creative?

What makes Sky Time Machine creative is its idea of turning astronomical observations into a time-based exploration experience. Instead of only displaying static astronomical images, the application allows users to compare different observation frames and visualize changes using Image Subtraction. This makes it easier to notice possible moving objects against the background of stars. Another interesting feature is the combination of 102 infrared spectral bands with interactive visualization, allowing users to explore how the sky appears at different wavelengths. I also included target presets and URL-sharing features to make the application easier to use. By combining these features in one platform, Sky Time Machine provides a different way to explore astronomical data that is both interactive and educational.

6. What factors did your team consider?

During the development of Sky Time Machine, we considered several important factors, especially user experience, scientific relevance, and application performance. First, we wanted to make sure that the application was easy to understand and navigate, even for users who do not have much experience with astronomy. Second, we focused on making the project relevant to the SPHEREx mission by including features related to its 102 infrared spectral bands and astronomical observation comparisons. We also considered performance and code organization by separating the application into different Python files, such as `sky_engine.py` and `sky_viewer.py`, so that each part has its own function and can be improved more easily. Overall, we wanted to create an application that is not only interesting to explore but also useful for learning and understanding astronomical data.
